findings.problem: fs::read_to_string(path).unwrap() — unwrap() on fallible I/O is a forbidden construct that panics on any read error
findings.failure_mode: Unreadable file, permission denied, or path errors abort the entire process instead of returning a typed error the caller can handle
findings.fix: Return a typed Result<Record, JobError> (e.g. JobError::Io(io::Error)) and propagate with ? through the caller

findings.problem: parts[1].parse::<u32>().unwrap() — unwrap() on fallible parse panics on non-numeric input
findings.failure_mode: A malformed CSV line with non-numeric second field causes a panic instead of returning a ParseError
findings.fix: Use parts[1].parse::<u32>().map_err(|e| JobError::Parse(e)) and propagate the error through the Result chain

findings.problem: lossy as cast from u32 to u16 — as u16 silently truncates values > 65535
findings.failure_mode: A valid u32 value like 70000 is silently truncated to 63536, silently corrupting data with no error reported
findings.fix: Use u16::try_from(parsed_u32).map_err(|_| JobError::ValueOutOfRange) or parse directly as u16 and check the range

findings.problem: parts[0] — unchecked indexing into a Vec with no bounds check
findings.failure_mode: Empty lines or lines with fewer than 2 comma-separated fields panic with index-out-of-bounds
findings.fix: Use parts.first() or split_once(',') and handle the None case by skipping or returning a ParseError

findings.problem: parts[1] — unchecked indexing into a Vec with no bounds check before accessing second field
findings.failure_mode: Lines with only one comma-separated field panic with index-out-of-bounds
findings.fix: Check parts.len() >= 2 or use parts.get(1) before parsing, returning a typed parse/field-missing error

findings.problem: println!("loaded {}", parts[0]) — I/O side effect embedded in data-loading logic
findings.failure_mode: Logging is mixed into the data pipeline, making the function non-deterministic, impossible to test in isolation, and coupling the core to console output
findings.fix: Remove println! from load_jobs. If logging is needed, return a separate metadata field or handle logging in the imperative shell at the call site

findings.problem: load_jobs mixes I/O (fs::read_to_string), parsing, logging, and data construction in a single function returning Vec — no clear separation of concerns
findings.failure_mode: Cannot unit-test the parsing/validating core without spawning real filesystem I/O and capturing console output; violations of illegal states go undetected because raw String fields are exposed publicly
findings.fix: Split into: (1) a pure fn parse_record(line: &str) -> Result<Record, ParseError> that takes &str and returns a validated Record; (2) an action fn load_jobs(path: &str) -> Result<Vec<Record>, JobError> that reads the file, calls parse_record per line, and handles errors

findings.problem: pub struct Record with pub name: String and pub value: u16 — raw public fields allow construction of invalid records
findings.failure_mode: Callers can construct Record { name: String::new(), value: 0 } or Record { name: "".into(), value: 0 } which may violate domain invariants (empty name, zero value); no type-level guarantee that values are in valid range
findings.fix: Make fields private and provide a fn new(name: String, value: u16) -> Result<Record, RecordError> that validates invariants; or use newtypes for domain-constrained values

findings.problem: fs::read_to_string is a blocking I/O call hidden inside a fn returning Vec<Record> — no Result, no async, no indication of fallibility in the signature
findings.failure_mode: The function signature claims to return Vec<Record> but can actually panic; callers have no way to handle I/O failures, and the blocking call can starve an async runtime if used in one
findings.fix: Change signature to fn load_jobs(path: &str) -> Result<Vec<Record>, JobError> (or use async fn) so fallibility is explicit in the type

findings.problem: load_jobs collects into Vec<Record> with no try_reserve or capacity hint, and per-line Vec<String> allocations on every line
findings.failure_mode: Unbounded memory growth on large files; repeated per-line Vec allocations add allocation pressure and potential OOM; no graceful handling of allocation failure
findings.fix: Estimate capacity from file metadata or line count, call Vec::try_reserve before collecting, and use &str slices with split_once instead of collecting parts into Vec<String>

findings.problem: No benchmarks, no profiler evidence, no allocation metrics — the function performs file I/O, string splitting, per-line allocation, parsing, and logging with zero performance measurement
findings.failure_mode: Cannot determine if this is suitable for hot paths, large files, or constrained memory environments; performance-regression-prone design with no baseline to validate against
findings.fix: Add a criterion/benchmark measuring throughput (lines/sec), allocation count, and memory usage for typical and edge-case inputs; add an allocation audit with #[global_allocator] tracking or dhat-rs

missing_evidence: no benchmark exists — no throughput, latency, or allocation baseline for load_jobs
no profiler evidence — hot path is not profiled for CPU hotspots in the parsing loop
no allocation analysis — no evidence that per-line Vec<String> allocations are bounded or minimal
no command evidence — cargo check, clippy, and test gates have not been executed
no tests — no unit tests, integration tests, or behavior tests exist for any parsing path or error case
residual_risk: Static review only — no commands run. All 10 findings are BLOCKERs requiring repair before delivery. The function as written violates multiple Holzman Rust non-negotiables: unwrap() on I/O and parse, unchecked indexing, lossy as cast, hidden I/O in the core path, no functional core/shell separation, public mutable fields enabling illegal states, no bounded allocation, and zero performance or test evidence.
